reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: A locally aggressive adnexal carcinoma with both follicular and eccrine/sweat-duct differentiation, favouring the central face and upper lip
Clinically deceptive, presenting as a slowly enlarging indurated flesh-coloured plaque or nodule that appears far more innocuous than its infiltrative behaviour
Histology reveals a paradox of deceptively bland superficial keratocysts and cords overlying a deeply infiltrative sclerosing component with marked perineural invasion
Perineural invasion is a hallmark and may cause paraesthesiae, numbness, or a burning sensation and contributes to deep subclinical extension
Superficial or shave biopsy is frequently non-diagnostic because it samples only the bland upper portion, so deep incisional biopsy is preferred
Because subclinical spread greatly exceeds clinical margins, Mohs micrographic surgery is the preferred treatment to achieve complete clearance
Distant metastasis is uncommon, but local recurrence after inadequate excision is frequent owing to the infiltrative and perineural growth
reference.pathophysiology: Microcystic adnexal carcinoma is a malignant adnexal tumour displaying dual follicular and sweat-duct (eccrine) differentiation. It is characterised by a striking zonation: the superficial portion comprises bland keratin-filled microcysts and small basaloid nests, while the deeper portion consists of infiltrating cords and ductal structures set in a dense sclerotic stroma. The tumour extends far beyond its apparent clinical borders, tracks along nerves (perineural invasion), and may invade underlying muscle, cartilage, and bone. This discrepancy between an indolent appearance and aggressive infiltrative local behaviour underlies both the frequent misdiagnosis on superficial biopsy and the high rate of local recurrence when margins are inadequate.
additionalDifferentials: Squamous cell carcinoma with ductal features
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional biopsy reaching the reticular dermis or subcutis rather than a superficial shave
Histopathology assessing depth of infiltration and perineural invasion
Immunohistochemistry to help distinguish from morphoeic basal cell carcinoma and desmoplastic trichoepithelioma
Mohs micrographic surgery with intraoperative margin mapping
Imaging to evaluate deep, bony, or perineural extension in advanced lesions
Neurological assessment when perineural symptoms are present
redFlags: Indurated facial plaque with sensory symptoms suggesting perineural invasion
Persistent or recurrent lesion after apparently adequate excision
Fixation to deeper structures suggesting muscle, cartilage, or bone involvement
Progressive facial numbness, pain, or motor deficit indicating nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: The tumour rarely metastasises but is notorious for extensive subclinical local infiltration and perineural spread, giving a high local recurrence rate after conventional excision; margin-controlled surgery substantially reduces recurrence, and long-term follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Relying on a superficial biopsy that samples only the bland upper tumour and misdiagnosing a benign lesion
Confusing it histologically with desmoplastic trichoepithelioma or morphoeic basal cell carcinoma
Underestimating margins and performing narrow excision, leading to recurrence
Ignoring perineural symptoms that signal deep nerve involvement
management: Complete surgical excision is the standard of care for localized disease whenever feasible.
Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred over wide local excision where available, since it allows full margin assessment and has a lower reported recurrence rate.
When wide local excision is used, margins may need to be generous (reports range from a few millimeters up to 3 to 5 cm) because subclinical extension is unpredictable.
MRI can help assess deep or perineural extension before surgery when clinically suspected, but a negative scan does not rule out subclinical spread.
Adequately deep biopsy (not a superficial shave) is essential before treatment planning, since superficial sampling can miss the infiltrative component and lead to misdiagnosis.

Radiotherapy can be used as adjuvant treatment after incomplete or high-risk surgical margins, or as monotherapy in patients who are not surgical candidates, with wide treatment margins to cover perineural spread.
Evidence for radiotherapy is limited to case reports and small series rather than large trials.
No established chemotherapy or targeted-therapy regimen exists for this disease, and metastasis is rare enough that routine systemic staging is not part of standard management.

For rare unresectable, recurrent, or metastatic disease, systemic therapy or clinical trial enrollment should be individualized at a center with head and neck or cutaneous oncology and multidisciplinary tumor board input.
Lifelong periodic examination of the skin and regional lymph nodes is recommended, since late local recurrence can occur decades after treatment.
Surveillance intervals and use of imaging should be individualized based on margin status, perineural invasion, and anatomic site.
Refer to a Mohs surgeon or center with Mohs capability whenever feasible given its favorable recurrence profile.
Refer for radiation oncology evaluation when margins cannot be cleared surgically, perineural invasion is extensive, or radiotherapy is being considered.
Refer to a multidisciplinary head and neck or cutaneous oncology team for suspected deep invasion, cranial nerve involvement, or confirmed metastatic disease.
